Name: Michelle Corbin
Badge: Layering Reading, Writing and Thinking
How does the Layering Reading, Writing, and Discussion approach compare to how you have previously supported students in engaging with multiple texts or teaching argument writing? How might this process shift or refine the way you guide students toward forming their own claims?:

I have definitely learned through this process that giving resources from the beginning in order to broaden the thoughts and opinions of my students helps them to read deeper, reflect on their thinking, and open their minds to different perspectives. It is silly to think that I presented my students with a question -- usually a topic I knew they knew some things about - and then expected them to make an informed decision about their thinking BEFORE the actual research and fact-finding took place. So many times, kids would write something through argumentative writing, only to tell me after that they had changed their thinking through their reading.

How would you describe the role of talk and discussion in your classroom right now? What kinds of opportunities do students have to rehearse ideas through conversation? What challenges have you encountered in making talk a meaningful part of the writing process?:
In my classroom, talk and discussion play an important but carefully managed role in the learning process. In previous years, when I used circle tables, I noticed that students engaged in a high level of conversation; however, much of it was not always academically focused. While collaboration is valuable, the structure sometimes led to off-task discussions. Middle schoolers!! This year, I shifted to rectangular tables, which has allowed for more flexibility for me and the kids. Students can face forward during direct instruction, but they also have the option to turn and engage in partner or small group discussions when appropriate. This change has helped create a better balance between independent focus and collaborative talk. Currently, students have structured opportunities to rehearse their ideas through conversation, particularly during partner discussions, small group work, and pre-writing activities. I often incorporate “turn and talk” moments, where students can process a question or respond to a prompt before writing. These opportunities allow students to clarify their thinking, hear different perspectives, and build confidence in their ideas. I’ve found that when students are given time to verbally process first, their written responses tend to be more developed and thoughtful. Despite these opportunities, I have encountered challenges in making talk a consistently meaningful part of the writing process. One ongoing challenge is ensuring that conversations stay focused and purposeful. Even with improved seating arrangements, some students still struggle to stay on task or may default to surface-level responses rather than deeper discussion. Another challenge is helping students understand how to transfer their verbal ideas into written form. So many ideas get lost in this process. While many students can articulate their thinking during discussion, they do not always carry that same depth into their writing without additional support. I have to remind them, in many instances, what exactly was said. To address these challenges, Sentence stems are a big part of the writing that we do. So much so, that kids ask where they are whenever I have forgotten to post them. Overall, I see talk as a valuable tool for developing student thinking, but one that requires intentional planning and structure.
